Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Corp.

DECLARATION AND SCOPE OF THIS SECTION 409A PAYMENT-TIMING INFORMATION SHEET
This Section 409A Payment-Timing Information Sheet is prepared with respect to Jordan Lee's employment with Acme Corp., which ended on September 4, 2026. It addresses federal tax law under Internal Revenue Code section 409A as it applies to separation pay and other nonqualified deferred compensation payable upon termination of employment, described in this document as arising under: 2024 Executive Severance Plan. It states what section 409A's own text, and the Treasury regulations issued under it, say about which events may trigger payment of such compensation, the additional delay that applies to certain employees of publicly traded corporations, two regulatory exemptions from section 409A's deferred-compensation timing rules, and the tax consequences of a violation. This document states facts about how federal tax law treats nonqualified deferred compensation in general; it does not determine whether any specific payment described in this document is or is not subject to section 409A, does not calculate any tax, and does not state what Jordan Lee or Acme Corp. should do about their situation.

"NONQUALIFIED DEFERRED COMPENSATION PLAN" DEFINED
Internal Revenue Code section 409A applies to a "nonqualified deferred compensation plan," a term the statute defines broadly, by exclusion, rather than by a positive list of arrangements it covers. The statute defines the term to mean any plan that provides for the deferral of compensation, other than a "qualified employer plan" (a category that includes tax-qualified retirement plans, certain eligible governmental deferred compensation plans, and certain excess benefit plans, each separately defined elsewhere in the same subsection) and other than any bona fide vacation leave, sick leave, compensatory time, disability pay, or death benefit plan. The statute further provides that the term "plan" includes any agreement or arrangement, including an agreement or arrangement that includes only one person -- meaning an individually negotiated severance or separation agreement can itself be a "plan" for these purposes, not only a formal, multi-participant benefit program.

SEPARATION FROM SERVICE AS A PERMITTED PAYMENT-TRIGGERING EVENT
Section 409A does not allow a nonqualified deferred compensation plan to distribute deferred compensation whenever the plan or the parties later choose. The statute instead requires that the plan itself provide that compensation deferred under it may not be distributed earlier than one of six specific events or times the statute lists: separation from service (as determined by the Secretary of the Treasury); the date the participant becomes disabled, within a further statutory meaning; death; a specified time, or a schedule fixed under the plan at the time the compensation was deferred; to the extent provided by the Secretary, a change in the ownership or effective control of the corporation, or in the ownership of a substantial portion of its assets; or the occurrence of an unforeseeable emergency. "Separation from service" is listed first among these six permitted triggers, and is the event most directly relevant to separation pay -- compensation a plan makes payable because employment with Acme Corp. ended.

THE SIX-MONTH DELAY FOR A "SPECIFIED EMPLOYEE" OF A PUBLICLY TRADED CORPORATION
Section 409A imposes an additional timing restriction on separation pay owed to a "specified employee." For any specified employee, the statute provides that the separation-from-service permitted-timing rule described above is met only if the plan does not permit distribution before the date that is six months after the date of separation from service, or, if earlier, the date of the employee's death. The statute defines a "specified employee," for this purpose, as a key employee -- as defined in a cross-referenced statute, without regard to one of that statute's own paragraphs -- of a corporation any stock in which is publicly traded on an established securities market or otherwise. This delay therefore applies only where two conditions are both met: the individual is a key employee within that cross-referenced definition, and the paying corporation's stock is publicly traded; the statute states no comparable six-month delay for a specified employee of a privately held corporation, because a privately held corporation's stock is not publicly traded on an established securities market or otherwise.

TWO REGULATORY EXEMPTIONS: THE "SHORT-TERM DEFERRAL" RULE AND THE "SEPARATION PAY PLAN" EXCEPTION
Section 409A's own statutory text does not define a "short-term deferral" exemption or a "separation pay plan" exemption; both are found instead in Treasury regulations issued under the statute's grant of regulatory authority. The short-term deferral regulation provides that a deferral of compensation does not occur under a plan with respect to a payment that is not a "deferred payment," provided that the service provider actually or constructively receives the payment on or before the last day of a specific window measured from when the compensation is no longer subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture -- a window the regulation defines as the period ending on the later of the 15th day of the third month following the end of the service provider's first taxable year in which the right to the payment is no longer subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture, or the 15th day of the third month following the end of the service recipient's (employer's) corresponding taxable year. Separately, the separation pay plan regulation provides that a separation pay plan that is not collectively bargained, and that provides separation pay only upon an involuntary separation from service or under a window program, does not provide for a deferral of compensation subject to section 409A to the extent the separation pay meets two conditions stated in the regulation: the amount does not exceed two times the lesser of the employee's annualized compensation for the preceding taxable year or the compensation limit applicable to qualified plans under a further cross-referenced statute for the year of separation, and the plan provides that the payment must be made no later than the last day of the second taxable year following the taxable year in which the separation from service occurs.

THE CONSEQUENCE OF A SECTION 409A VIOLATION: INCOME INCLUSION, A 20% ADDITIONAL TAX, AND INTEREST
Section 409A attaches severe consequences where a nonqualified deferred compensation plan fails to meet, or is not operated in accordance with, its distribution-timing, no-acceleration, and election-timing requirements. The statute provides that if at any time during a taxable year the plan fails or is not operated in compliance, all compensation deferred under the plan for that taxable year and all preceding taxable years is includible in the affected participants' gross income for that taxable year, to the extent not already subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture and not previously included in gross income -- not merely the specific payment that was mistimed. Beyond this accelerated income inclusion, the statute imposes two further, separately calculated amounts on top of the participant's regular income tax on that amount: interest, computed at the underpayment rate plus one percentage point, calculated as if the deferred compensation had been included in income when it was first deferred (or, if later, when it first became free of a substantial risk of forfeiture); and an additional tax equal to 20 percent of the compensation required to be included in gross income under this rule.

expectedJSON.body: Section 409A attaches severe consequences where a nonqualified deferred compensation plan fails to meet, or is not operated in accordance with, its distribution-timing, no-acceleration, and election-timing requirements. The statute provides that if at any time during a taxable year the plan fails or is not operated in compliance, all compensation deferred under the plan for that taxable year and all preceding taxable years is includible in the affected participants' gross income for that taxable year, to the extent not already subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture and not previously included in gross income -- not merely the specific payment that was mistimed. Beyond this accelerated income inclusion, the statute imposes two further, separately calculated amounts on top of the participant's regular income tax on that amount: interest, computed at the underpayment rate plus one percentage point, calculated as if the deferred compensation had been included in income when it was first deferred (or, if later, when it first became free of a substantial risk of forfeiture); and an additional tax equal to 20 percent of the compensation required to be included in gross income under this rule.

citations.quote: all compensation deferred under the plan for the taxable year and all preceding taxable years shall be includible in gross income for the taxable year to the extent not subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture and not previously included in gross income.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 409A(a)(1)(B)(i) (Inclusion in gross income of deferred compensation under nonqualified deferred compensation plans -- interest and 20% additional tax)
citations.quote: the tax imposed by this chapter for the taxable year shall be increased by the sum of—

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 409A(a)(1)(B)(i)(II) (Inclusion in gross income of deferred compensation under nonqualified deferred compensation plans -- 20 percent additional tax amount)
citations.quote: an amount equal to 20 percent of the compensation which is required to be included in gross income.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 409A(a)(1)(B)(ii) (Inclusion in gross income of deferred compensation under nonqualified deferred compensation plans -- interest calculation)
citations.quote: the interest determined under this clause for any taxable year is the amount of interest at the underpayment rate plus 1 percentage point on the underpayments that would have occurred had the deferred compensation been includible in gross income for the taxable year in which first deferred or, if later, the first taxable year in which such deferred compensation is not subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause cites subdivisions of a single statutory subsection, 26 U.S.C. § 409A(a)(1) -- the income-inclusion rule at § 409A(a)(1)(A)(i), and the interest-and-20%-tax rule at § 409A(a)(1)(B)(i) and (ii), are part of that one subsection and are not independent sources of each other. This clause does not restate § 409A(a)(1)(A)(ii), which limits this consequence to participants "with respect to whom the failure relates" rather than every participant in the plan, and it does not address the separate funding-related consequences under § 409A(b) for offshore trusts or restricted-fund arrangements, which involve different triggering conduct (funding mechanics rather than distribution timing) and a different consequence provision this document does not cover. It does not determine whether any specific plan or payment described in this document has in fact violated section 409A, and it does not calculate the amount of any tax, interest, or income inclusion that would result. This is federal tax law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule; it has no state-law analog and operates independently of any separate consequence state law may impose on the same payment.
